## Project Overview: Probability in the Wild

This quarter, you will follow **one public health scenario**. Each time we learn a new set of probability and simulation tools, you will apply them to your scenario in a checkpoint. At the end of the quarter, you will pull your checkpoints together into a short brief written for the public health program in your scenario.

Every checkpoint follows the same three steps:

1.  **Solve it:** Set up the problem with probability notation and solve it analytically (by hand or with R as a calculator).
2.  **Simulate it:** Write a simulation in R and check that it agrees with your analytic answer. If the two answers disagree, explain why.
3.  **Say it:** Interpret your results in plain language for someone who is not a statistician.

You may work **alone or in pairs**. If you work in a pair, you keep the same partner and scenario for the whole quarter.

### Scenario menu

Pick one of the three scenarios below. Each one comes with a fixed setting and a short packet of published sources, so you do not need to search for sources yourself. The full scenario cards are in [Checkpoint 0](/project/Checkpoint_00_instructions.qmd#scenario-cards). You may propose your own scenario only with my approval (see Checkpoint 0).

| Scenario | CP 1: Conditional probability & Bayes | CP 2: Discrete RV | CP 3: Continuous RV & CLT |
|----|----|----|----|
| A. Community breast cancer screening program | P(cancer \| abnormal mammogram) | Follow-up appointments needed after a van day of 40 screens | Size of a tumor found by screening |
| B. County COVID-19 testing and contact tracing | P(infected \| positive rapid test) | Household contacts of a case who get infected | Incubation period |
| C. State newborn heart screening program | P(heart defect \| positive pulse oximetry screen) | Babies born with a heart defect in the state in a year | Birth weight |

::: callout-note
## Use real numbers

Every input value (prevalence, sensitivity, rate, mean, etc.) comes from your scenario's source packet or from a course value on your scenario card. Cite the source each time you use a value. You do not need to analyze a dataset. The data in this project come from simulation.
:::

## Final Project: Public Health Brief

**The final project is due `r proj %>% format("%m/%d")`.**

In the final project, you will revise your three checkpoints based on feedback and combine them into one story about your scenario. You will submit:

1.  **Technical appendix:** Your revised Checkpoints 1–3 in a single rendered Quarto file.
2.  **Public health brief:** A 2-page brief (or a 5-minute recorded explanation) for the manager of the public health program in your scenario. It should answer: *What does probability tell us about this program, and what should the manager keep in mind when making decisions?*

The [Final Project Instructions](/project/Final_Project_instructions.qmd) describe both pieces, what each section of the brief should include, and the rubric.
